messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Unemployed
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 75

Martha is a fifty-eight-year-old woman who lives alone in the two-bedroom bungalow she shared with her husband, Frank, for thirty-two years. She has been unemployed since the summer of 2021, when she was let go from her position as a medical records clerk at the local hospital. She tells me this happened “around the same time everything else fell apart,” though she cannot say exactly when she stopped going to work versus when she stopped caring.

The trauma happened on a Tuesday in late June. Frank, a retired electrician, had been feeling tired for a few weeks. Martha had nagged him to see the doctor. He finally agreed, and she drove him to the appointment. In the examining room, the doctor spoke in a calm, measured voice about the CT scan results. Pancreatic cancer. Stage four. Martha remembers the word “inoperable.” She remembers Frank’s hand going still on the armrest of the chair. She remembers the doctor saying something about six months, maybe eight if they tried certain therapies. What she does not remember is driving home. She does not remember the next three days. She only knows that at some point in the following week, she found herself standing in the kitchen at 3:00 AM, staring at the microwave clock, unable to recall how she got there.

Frank died eleven weeks later. Martha was with him. She held his hand. She watched his chest stop moving. She tells me this part without emotion, as if reading from a chart. Then she is quiet for a long moment, and her right hand begins to tremble slightly, resting on her knee. She does not look at me when she says, “I keep seeing his face when the doctor said the word. That look. I can’t stop seeing it.”

Since Frank’s death, Martha has been unable to watch television. The news is unbearable. She cannot listen to the radio. She cannot sit in the living room because the recliner where Frank used to sit is still there, and sometimes she glances at it and expects to see him. She has not touched his side of the closet. She sleeps on the couch now, in the den, because the bedroom is too quiet. She wakes up multiple times a night, her heart pounding, convinced she heard his voice calling her name. She does not check. She just lies still, waiting for the feeling to pass.

She stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent lights make her feel trapped. She orders delivery, but sometimes she forgets to eat. She has lost twenty-three pounds. Her daughter, who lives two hours away, calls every evening. Martha lets the phone ring. She texts back “fine” so her daughter will not worry. The truth is she has not left the house in eleven days. She tells me she is not sad, exactly. She is hollow. She is waiting. She does not know for what.

There are moments during our sessions when Martha’s eyes go distant, and she stops mid-sentence. She tells me she has been having what she calls “replays.” A sound—the hum of a refrigerator, the clatter of a dish—will trigger a full sensory memory of the doctor’s office. The smell of hand sanitizer. The texture of the vinyl chair. The precise tone of the doctor’s voice. She feels the same panic she felt that day, the same cold sweat, the same sense that the floor is tilting. She has learned to keep her eyes on the ground during these episodes, because looking up makes the room spin.

She says the worst part is not the sadness. It is the feeling that she is still in that room, still hearing those words, and that everything since—the funeral, the empty house, the long afternoons—has been a dream she cannot wake from. She has stopped answering the door. She has stopped checking the mail. She sits in the den with the curtains drawn, and she waits for the replays to stop, even though she knows they will not.
